findings.matters: Changes to what the DfE will allow to be charged to the High Needs Block are affecting several councils, and this paper quantifies the general fund impact.

findings.figures: The paper states no amount for the EFS borrowing requirement. Other Long-Term Liabilities are forecast at £115.984m against an approved £174.949m
findings.quote: as well as to fund borrowing for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.headline: Total long-term external borrowing of £547.071m at 30 September 2026, down from £564.171m at 31 March 2026, with average rate 3.25%
findings.detail: The paper's table shows the General Fund portfolio at £342.200m (average rate 2.92%) and the HRA portfolio at £204.871m (average rate 4.19%). All PWLB loans are at fixed rates, and the market loans and bond are unchanged.
findings.matters: The fall in outstanding debt and the drop in average rate from 3.28% to 3.25% show the portfolio's cost position moving at a time when the paper forecasts higher PWLB rates.

findings.headline: £17.1m of maturing PWLB debt repaid by 30 September 2026
findings.detail: The paper states that a further £42m of maturing PWLB debt is due by the end of March, and that new external borrowing will be needed for capital expenditure funded by borrowing and for Exceptional Financial Support. The paper's date for the £42m reads 'March 2026', while other sections refer to the 2026/27 year.
findings.matters: Repayments and the further £42m due show how much replacement funding the council must source from the PWLB or market, which other councils and lenders will want to compare.
findings.figures: £17.1m PWLB debt repaid; £42m further maturing PWLB debt
findings.quote: As at 30 September 2026, £17.1m of maturing PWLB debt has been repaid with a further £42m due by end of March 2026.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio of £129.500m at 30 September 2026 forecast to reduce to £79.080m by 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The paper attributes the forecast fall to historic spending patterns, the current year capital programme, the forecast EFS borrowing requirement and decisions on the level of external borrowing. It notes that cash balances include amounts belonging to schools, the HRA, the Pension Fund and third parties.
findings.matters: A forecast halving of cash balances within six months is the kind of liquidity change a lender or peer finance team will want to track against the council's stated minimum cash requirement.
findings.figures: £129.500m at 30 September 2026; £79.080m forecast at 31 March 2027; £143.800m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: This is forecast will reduce to £79.080m by the end of the year, based on historic spending patterns

findings.headline: CCLA property fund investment valued at £17.070m at 30 September 2026 against £20.000m invested, a capital depreciation of 14.65%
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall in value mainly to inflation and interest rates affecting real estate capital values across the sector. It states that a government statutory override now reverses unrealised fair value movements from pooled investment funds, and that the fund continues to generate income.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council holding a similar pooled property fund will want to see how a 14.65% fall against cost is being reported and how the statutory override is being applied.
findings.figures: £17.070m bid value; £20.000m invested; 14.65% capital depreciation; 258 local authorities invest in the fund
findings.quote: As at the 30 September the bid value (sale / fair value) of the Council’s investment in the CCLA property fund was £17.070m, a ca pital depreciation of 14.65% against the Council’s investment of £20.000m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Borrowing as at 31 March 26
findings.headline: Portfolio shifting from PWLB-dominated (85%) to market-dependent (100%) as £479m PWLB is fully repaid without replacement.
findings.detail: Opening balance shows £479.171m PWLB (85% of £564.171m total) and £85m market/bond (15%). Repayment schedules show £504.171m PWLB being fully amortized while £589.171m market/bond is managed through refinancing. Council is transitioning to full market financing.
findings.matters: Shift from fixed-rate PWLB to market-rate debt changes interest rate exposure; market-dependent financing carries greater refinancing and pricing risk than PWLB access.
findings.figures: Opening PWLB: £479,171,000; Opening market/bond: £85,000,000; PWLB total repayment: £504,171,000; Market/bond total repayment: £589,171,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Borrowing as at 31 March 26
findings.headline: £75m refinancing required in 2069/70 represents 12.73% of total portfolio and the largest future debt event 43 years out.
findings.detail: Market/bond debt repayments are scheduled through 2069/70. The final year shows £75m of borrowing due, the single largest refinancing event in the projection. Portfolio maturity extends 43 years from the report date, creating long-dated refinancing obligations.
findings.matters: Refinancing needs four decades ahead create sustained interest rate risk and refinancing risk; the council must maintain capital markets access and investor confidence over an unusually extended period.
findings.figures: £75,000,000 scheduled for 2069/70; represents 12.73% of total portfolio; portfolio matures across 43-year period

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Borrowing as at 31 March 26
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing ends after 2026/27; no further PWLB access planned despite £479m existing PWLB stock.
findings.detail: The council is taking £25m PWLB borrowing in 2026/27, after which the PWLB borrow column shows '-' (zero) for all subsequent years through 2069/70. The entire PWLB portfolio of £504.171m total will be repaid with no replacement from PWLB sources. This signals either PWLB capacity exhaustion (potentially due to Exceptional Finance Provision restrictions) or a deliberate shift to market financing.
findings.matters: PWLB is typically cheaper than market funding; loss of access increases future borrowing costs and signals the council is now dependent on capital markets for any refinancing or new borrowing.
findings.figures: £25,000,000 PWLB borrowing in 2026/27 only; £504,171,000 total PWLB principal (£479,171,000 opening plus £25,000,000 new); zero PWLB borrowing from 2027/28 onward

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Investment balances fell by £27m to £116.800m as council deployed cash for capital funding
findings.detail: The council's available-for-investment cash balances decreased from £143.800m to £116.800m over the year. Per the council's explanation, this was partly due to timing differences in cash flows but primarily due to temporary deployment of internal resources to fund the capital programme, consistent with the deliberate under-borrowing strategy.
findings.matters: Depletion of liquid reserves indicates the council is consuming its cash buffer to avoid external borrowing. While deliberate, this reduces flexibility and liquidity headroom for unforeseen demands.
findings.figures: Investment balances £116.800m (31/03/26) vs £143.800m (31/03/25), decrease of £27m (19% reduction)
findings.quote: The overall level of cash balances decreased by £27m, this was due in part to timing differences between the receipt and payment of cash transactions, and the temporary use of internal resources to fund the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: No PWLB debt rescheduling opportunities identified despite annual portfolio review; refinancing windows closed
findings.detail: The council kept its borrowing portfolio under review throughout 2025/26 and considered debt rescheduling opportunities, but determined that no cost-beneficial options existed. The interest rate differential between current loan rates and replacement rates was insufficient to justify refinancing action. This indicates the PWLB rate structure is not moving favourably for the council.
findings.matters: Absence of refinancing opportunities indicates interest rates are not moving in the council's favour; the council remains locked into its current debt stack and cannot improve its cost position through market activity.
findings.figures: Zero PWLB loans rescheduled or prematurely repaid in 2025/26
findings.quote: No PWLB loans were rescheduled or prematurely repaid. This was because the PWLB interest rate differential between the actual loan rate and repayment loan rate would not have provided a cost benefit to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account affordability deteriorated to 17.92%, driven by new £35m borrowing at 4.25%
findings.detail: The ratio of HRA financing costs to net revenue stream increased from 14.79% to 17.92%. This reflects new borrowing of £35m taken during 2025/26 at 4.25% (reflecting HRA certainty rate), combined with principal repayments of £24.5m. HRA debt stands at £219.621m across 4,838 dwellings, with debt per dwelling at £0.045m.
findings.matters: HRA affordability above 15% represents regulatory attention point. Rising HRA financing costs constrain available resources for responsive repairs, planned maintenance and new housing delivery. This trajectory warrants monitoring.
findings.figures: HRA ratio 17.92% (2025/26) vs 14.79% (2024/25); HRA debt £219.621m; new PWLB borrowing £35m at 4.25%; debt per dwelling £0.045m
findings.quote: The reason for the increase in HRA ratio is due to increase in borrowing and its associated finance cost.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Investment portfolio achieved 4.75% return, outperforming 4.05% benchmark by 70 basis points
findings.detail: The council's £116.8m of investment balances generated average returns of 4.75% against a benchmark of the 1-month SONIA rate at 4.05%. The CCLA strategic property fund holding contributed 4.61% yield. Short-term money market funds and fixed term deposits provided the bulk of liquid returns.
findings.matters: Investment outperformance of 70bps generates material additional revenue income that offsets debt servicing costs and protects the revenue budget. This demonstrates effective cash management during volatile interest rate conditions.
findings.figures: 4.75% actual return vs 4.05% benchmark; CCLA fund yield 4.61%; investment portfolio £116.800m
findings.quote: The average rate of return of 4.75% was above the benchmark return of 4.05%.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowing position of £94.934m, using internal resources to defer external financing
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (underlying borrowing need) was £749.253m as at 31 March 2026, but long-term external borrowing was only £679.067m. This £94.934m gap represents internal resources (cash reserves) deployed as a substitute for external debt. The Treasury Management Strategy explicitly approves this approach to maintain flexibility while awaiting more favorable rate environments.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing shows confidence in future refinancing but creates liquidity vulnerability if reserves are drawn down for service pressures or capital acceleration. The internal resource buffer is finite.
findings.figures: Internal resources deployed: £94.934m; Capital Financing Requirement £749.253m; external borrowing £679.067m
findings.quote: Long term external borrowing amounted to £679.067m, therefore an estimated total of £94.934m of internal resources have been utilised in lieu of external borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Average cost of borrowing increased to 3.53%, marking first annual rise in recent period
findings.detail: The council's long-term borrowing portfolio cost rose by 10 basis points. The council took £85m new PWLB loans for the General Fund and £35m for the Housing Revenue Account, both at higher rates than prior year debt. The 3.53% figure includes PWLB loans (80% of portfolio) at average 2.89% for GF and 4.19% for HRA, plus market loans and bonds.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs directly reduce the council's capacity to finance capital investment and compress revenue budgets. A 10bps annual increase compounds across the £564m borrowed base.
findings.figures: 3.53% (2025/26) vs 3.43% (2024/25), an increase of 0.10 percentage points; £85m PWLB GF at 2.89% average; £35m PWLB HRA at 4.25%
findings.quote: The Council's average long-term cost of borrowing was 3.53% an increase of 0.10% from the previous year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn 25-26 for Council - Report Final
findings.headline: Net borrowing increased by £119.487m to £447.371m in a single financial year
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing position (external debt minus investments) grew from £327.884m to £447.371m. External borrowing rose to £564.171m while investment balances fell to £116.800m. This represents a 36% increase in net debt position over 12 months.
findings.matters: A £119m increase in net borrowing in one year is material and represents a significant directional movement in the council's debt trajectory that affects credit risk and repayment capacity.
findings.quote: The net borrowing increased by £119.487m compared to last year.

findings.paper_title: LGPS Fit for the Future LBR Pension Fund Implementation Workplan - Report
findings.headline: Governance restructuring requires appointment of new Senior LGPS Officer and Independent Persons by 31 December 2026, with role separation restrictions.
findings.detail: New regulations require the Pension Fund to appoint a Senior LGPS Officer and Independent Persons by 31 December 2026. The regulations prohibit the Senior LGPS Officer from simultaneously being the Section 151 Officer, Monitoring Officer or Head of Paid Service, requiring the creation of a distinct governance role.
findings.matters: The council will likely need to create a new senior position to meet this requirement, with associated employment and implementation costs, and governance structure changes affect the fund's management capability.
findings.figures: 31 December 2026 deadline
findings.quote: Members should note that the Regulations prohibit the LGPS Senior Officer from simultaneously being the Section 151 Officer, Monitoring Officer or Head of Paid Service.

findings.paper_title: LGPS Fit for the Future LBR Pension Fund Implementation Workplan - Report
findings.headline: The council has seven days to execute the London CIV Investment Management Agreement or face regulatory scrutiny.
findings.detail: The Pension Fund must execute the Investment Management Agreement with London CIV by 30 September 2026. This agreement establishes the framework through which London CIV will implement the Fund's investment strategy. Failure to meet this deadline may result in non-compliance with the Government's pooling requirements and expose the Fund to regulatory scrutiny.
findings.matters: Missing a statutory deadline is a governance failure that could trigger regulatory action and undermine investor and stakeholder confidence in the fund's management.
findings.figures: 30 September 2026 deadline
findings.quote: The Fund must ensure that the IMA is agreed and executed by 30 September 2026. This milestone is important as it establishes the contractual framework through which London CIV will implement the Fund's investment strategy and supports compliance with the Government's pooling requirements.

findings.headline: HRA housing programme accelerated to £58.6m in 2026/27, up from originally planned £22.5m, funded from future years' approved provisions.
findings.detail: The Existing Social Housing Stock programme has been reprofiled to bring forward £36.5m of spend from future years into 2026/27 to "align approved investment with current commitments, statutory compliance obligations and identify asset needs". This significantly front-loads cash drawdown and changes the borrowing profile across years.
findings.matters: A £36.5m acceleration (63% increase to planned spend) materially changes the council's borrowing need and cash flow profile for 2026/27. This can require either accelerated drawdown of existing facilities or new borrowing headroom. The stated reasons (commitments, compliance, asset needs identification) suggest these may not be discretionary delays.
findings.figures: Existing Social Housing Stock: £22.5m originally planned → £58.598m 2026/27 forecast; acceleration of £36.500m; HRA total programme £72.800m in 2026/27 vs £72.800m across 2027/28–2030/31 combined
findings.quote: The programme has been accelerated to align approved investment with current commitments, statutory compliance obligations and identify asset needs. The 2026/27 budget is reprofiled from £22.5m to £58.598m funded from approved future years' provisions.

findings.headline: Wanstead High School main contractor has gone into administration, halting the £3.6m project with cost implications still under review.
findings.detail: The council's largest education capital project (£3.585m in Q1 budget) faces delivery failure at the contractor stage. The council is undertaking a review to determine both financial implications and completion cost. This creates both timing and cost risk on a project that was already forecast to run into 2028/29.
findings.matters: Contractor failure on a capital scheme of this scale typically results in cost overruns, delay penalties, and extended financing costs. The council has not yet quantified the exposure.
findings.figures: £3.585m Q1 budget; original maturity extended beyond 2026/27; £6.000m forecast spend in 2027/28 already approved
findings.quote: The main contractor for the Wanstead project has gone into administration, creating a further delay. The Council is currently undertaking a review to determine the financial implications of this, as well as the cost of completing the project.

findings.headline: RAAC building safety closures: South Woodford Library, Kenneth Moore Theatre, Fullwell Cross Leisure Centres creating £1.451m loss of income
findings.detail: Three facilities (South Woodford Library, Kenneth Moore Theatre, Fullwell Cross Leisure Centres) have been closed due to RAAC structural issues. The leisure provider is claiming £1.451m loss of income. Additionally, planned Fullwell Cross modernization is not proceeding, so budgeted income from membership fees is not being received. The council is also incurring costs for security and maintenance of closed facilities.
findings.matters: Closure of public facilities due to building safety issues (RAAC) signals aging infrastructure and deferred maintenance. Loss of income creates immediate revenue pressure. Unscheduled capital investment in remediation or replacement will compete for resources.
findings.figures: £1.451m loss of income claim, £0.045m red saving not happening (Fullwell Cross modernization not proceeding)
findings.quote: Pressures of £1.451m due to claim for loss of income as a result of temporary closure of South Woodford Library, Kenneth Moore Theatre and Fullwell Cross Leisure Centres.

findings.headline: Wanstead Pool and School capital project: contractor insolvent, £0.500m delay claims under dispute, £0.657m revenue costs for security and temporary classrooms
findings.detail: Contractor Jerram Falkus entered administration. The appointed administrators are pursuing two delay claims totalling £0.500m (which the council disputes). Pending resolution, the council is incurring £0.657m in revenue costs for security and temporary classroom hire, which are not eligible for capitalization. This revenue cost is flagged as one-off but represents immediate pressure.
findings.matters: Contractor insolvency creates legal liability and contingent payment risk. The £0.500m claimed delay cost, if awarded, would hit revenue budget. Interim costs of £0.657m erode financial headroom.
findings.figures: £0.500m potential delay claims (disputed), £0.657m revenue overspend for security and temporary classrooms
findings.quote: The contractor Jerram Falkus has become insolvent and entered into Administration and there is still a risk that the appointed Administrators may continue to pursue two recent delay claims that were presented to the Local Authority by the Contractor prior to entering Administration and totalling up to £0.500m. The Local Authority disputes these claims.

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities care packages £2.713m over budget; rising EHCP numbers and provider costs continuing
findings.detail: CWD support packages are £2.713m (19%) over budget, driven by rising numbers of children with complex additional needs and increased provider staffing costs. The overspend reflects rising Education Health & Care Plans identifying social care needs. The forecast includes ongoing pressures from this demand trend and does not assume this will reverse.
findings.matters: Rising EHCP numbers and increasing complexity of need is a national trend. The council's forecast worsening month-on-month (from £2.577m at M2 to £2.713m at Q1) suggests demand is outpacing planning assumptions, eroding financial control.
findings.figures: £2.713m CWD overspend, £0.136m adverse movement M2 to Q1, rising EHCP numbers identified as 'ongoing'
findings.quote: The projected overspend reflects the growth in children with complex additional needs (both local and national issues) and increased costs from providers due to increases in their staffing costs. The increase in demand also reflects the rising number of Education Health & Care Plans (EHCP) which have identified social care needs which have to be met.

findings.headline: Parking enforcement income £2.000m short; only £0.500m recovery expected from mitigations, leaving £1.500m residual shortfall
findings.detail: The parking account is forecasting £2.000m income shortfall driven by enforcement challenges, CCTV site-specific delays, and resourcing issues that have reduced PCN output. Debt recovery, planned to restart 1 April 2026, was delayed due to 'approval and operational readiness'. The council expects mitigations to recover only £0.500m through new CCTV sites and other actions, leaving £1.500m unrecovered.
findings.matters: Parking income is discretionary revenue. Material reliance on it to offset demand pressures signals revenue stress and reduced flexibility to absorb shocks. Delays in implementing debt recovery suggest operational readiness problems.
findings.figures: £2.000m shortfall, £0.300-0.400m debt recovery delay shortfall, £0.500m total mitigation, £1.500m residual shortfall
findings.quote: The parking account is currently forecasting a pressure of £2.000m primarily driven by a number of CCTV site related factors. These include enforcement challenges and site-specific issues (delay and removal of some locations) and resourcing issues which have collectively reduced expected output in terms of number of PCN's issued.

findings.headline: Adult social care client contribution income not being recovered: £1.636m nursing charges, £1.503m home care charges shortfall
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is £2.380m overspent. The key driver is non-recovery of budgeted client income: nursing charges (£1.636m) and home care services (£1.503m) are not being collected. This is coupled with pressures in care purchasing, agency homecare, mental health S117 cases, and supported living costs. The council is also investing £0.955m in additional CQC safeguarding staffing.
findings.matters: Non-recovery of client contributions is a structural income problem, not a temporary collection delay. Combined with rising care costs and demand, this indicates the council cannot sustain current social care models through user charges.
findings.figures: £1.636m nursing charges under-recovery, £1.503m home care under-recovery, £2.380m total Adults overspend, £0.955m CQC staffing costs
findings.quote: The variance is mainly due to projected under-recovery of income against the budget. Significant element of this is related to budgeted client income for Home Care services (£1.503m) and Nursing charges (£1.636m) along with pressures in ICB income.

findings.headline: High Needs Block funding withdrawals: £0.898m won't materialise; backdated adjustments to 2025/26; DSG override ends 2028
findings.detail: SEND transport High Needs Block contribution of £0.445m and REWTS funding of £0.453m are 'unlikely to take place following discussions with the Department for Education'. Both have backdated adjustments to 2025/26. The adverse movement in Education & Inclusion from M2 to Q1 is £1.290m, with £0.890m from SEN Transport alone. There is a further £0.536m identified risk of HNB costs transferring to General Fund. After 31 March 2028, the DSG Statutory Override ends and future DSG overspends must be funded from General Fund.
findings.matters: Unexpected withdrawal of expected funding creates an immediate budget cliff. With SEND demand continuing to rise and the DSG override ending in 2028, the council faces a structural funding shortfall in a growing cost area.
findings.figures: £0.445m HNB transport contribution withdrawn, £0.453m REWTS contribution withdrawn, £0.445m and £0.453m backdated adjustments, £0.536m risk of further transfers, £0.890m adverse movement in SEN transport M2 to Q1
findings.quote: the anticipated High Needs Block contribution to Personal Travel Budget (£0.445m) is unlikely to take place following discussions with the Department for Education with a back-dated adjustment (£0.445m) relating to 2025/26

findings.headline: Of £15.838m approved savings, £2.368m (14.95%) on track, £8.806m (55.6%) unconfirmed delivery, £4.369m (27.6%) undeliverable
findings.detail: The savings tracker shows 27.6% of savings marked Red (undeliverable), 55.6% Amber (at risk), 14.95% Green (on track). Place, Communities & Enterprise has only 14% of savings on track. Cross Council savings are only 3% on track, with £5.806m Amber. This pattern across all directorates indicates systemic delivery failure, not isolated issues.
findings.matters: A council's ability to balance budgets through cost control is a core measure of financial resilience. Widespread failure to deliver savings (83% of target not on track) indicates structural deficit and dependence on continued reserves drawdown or service cuts.
findings.figures: £15.838m total savings, £4.369m Red (27.59%), £8.806m Amber (55.60%), £2.368m Green (14.95%), Place 14% on track, Cross Council 3% on track
findings.quote: RAG Status as % of Savings Total 27.59% 55.60% 14.95% 1.86%

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation undeliverable savings: £3.242m restructuring plan delayed, households in TA growing
findings.detail: The Place, Communities & Enterprise directorate is £9.719m overspent, of which £3.252m is temporary accommodation. The council planned £3.242m in savings by converting expensive nightly lets to longer-term leases, but implementation is delayed 'due to a delay in the implementation of the design restructure'. TA household numbers are rising: 2,819 in April to 2,918 in June 2026. Nightly lets alone account for 1,214 households.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-driven cost the council cannot control without service delivery changes. A failed restructuring plan means the largest cost driver in the directorate is unmanageable, suggesting structural deficit risk and eroding reserves.
findings.figures: £3.252m overspend, £3.242m unachievable savings, 2,918 TA households in June 2026 (up from 2,819 in April), 1,214 nightly lets
findings.quote: The risks of under-delivery of the savings of c£3.242m is due to a delay in the implementation of the design restructure, converting expensive nightly lets to longer term leases with current providers with discussions in place currently with landlord providers and transitioning these arrangements to longer term leaseholds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Outturn HRA DSG - Q1 (1)
findings.headline: Government DSG funding support is conditional and time-limited; deficits will transfer to general fund when statutory override ends in 2028
findings.detail: The High Needs Stability Grant covers only 90% of eligible cumulative DSG deficits to end March 2026, and is conditional on submitting a satisfactory SEND reform plan. For 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits, government has indicated only proportionate support explicitly described as 'not unlimited'. Residual DSG deficit of £0.782m (plus £0.536m under DfE review) will require general fund cover, with no guarantee of continued support beyond 2028.
findings.matters: Creates a funding certainty cliff in 2028 when accumulated DSG deficits (potentially exceeding £26m) become an unfunded mandate on the general fund. Government support is explicitly limited and conditional on performance, creating budget risk.
findings.figures: £7.034m estimated High Needs Stability Grant (90% of £7.815m eligible to March 2026); £0.782m residual deficit requiring general fund cover; £0.536m additional amount under DfE review; £17.352m additional forecast deficit in 2026/27
findings.quote: If not mitigated this will need to be met from the General Fund when the statutory override ceases.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Outturn HRA DSG - Q1 (1)
findings.headline: Special school and independent placement costs rising faster than budget due to staffing and National Insurance pressures
findings.detail: Placement costs exceed forecast across all provision types. Non-maintained and independent special schools show the highest average top-up at £69,297 per place (111 pupils, £1.692m overspend); in-borough special schools average £30,423 per place (771 pupils, £5.803m overspend). The council explicitly states these pressures will intensify due to higher staffing costs from National Insurance contribution changes and sector-wide inflation.
findings.matters: Market-driven cost inflation creates structural deficits beyond the council's direct control; external pressures (NI contributions, sector wage inflation) indicate this is not cyclical and will persist.
findings.figures: Non-maintained/independent schools: 111 pupils at £69,297 average top-up (£1.692m overspend); in-borough special schools: 771 pupils at £30,423 average (£5.803m overspend); total special placement overspends £8.508m of the £17.352m total
findings.quote: market pressures continue to drive fee inflation. In 2026/27, these pressures are expected to intensify as providers experience higher staffing costs arising from changes to employer National Insurance Contributions and wider inflationary impacts across the sector.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Outturn HRA DSG - Q1 (1)
findings.headline: High Needs Block forecast to overspend by £17.352m in 2026/27, building cumulative DSG deficit to £26.487m
findings.detail: The DSG overspend is driven by growing numbers of children with EHCPs (3,799 pupils across all provision types) and increasing placement costs. The council notes that while funding has increased in recent years, these increases have not kept pace with EHCP growth or rising complexity of need. This creates a cumulative DSG deficit of £26.487m by 31 March 2027, up from £9.135m brought forward, with no forecast end in sight.
findings.matters: When the statutory override allowing separate DSG deficit accounting ends in 2028, accumulated DSG deficits must transfer to the general fund, creating a direct hit to the council's financial position and reducing capacity for debt service and other priorities.
findings.figures: £17.352m in-year overspend on £68.665m budget; cumulative DSG deficit of £26.487m by 31 March 2027 (up from £9.135m); 3,799 children supported across all SEND provision types
findings.quote: The High Needs Block (£68.665m) is forecasting an overspend of £17.352m.

findings.headline: Only 17% of planned £15.838m annual savings on track; 55.60% at amber and 14.95% off-track
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 savings programme totals £15.838m. Q1 assessment shows only 17% on track against the annual target. By RAG status: 27.59% of savings value is Green (on track), 55.60% Amber (at risk of non-delivery), and 14.95% Red (off track). findings.detail: MTFS explicitly identifies inflation and interest rates as remaining 'high for longer than previously anticipated' due to 'continued instability, particularly globally'. This creates dual pressure: increased operating costs for services, and increased costs for the substantial borrowing council plans to undertake through EFS capitalisation.

Multiple staffing changes (interim head); operational improvements plan still developing.
findings.matters: Service overseen by interim management; multiple control/improvement actions stalled; reliance on manual processes and incomplete digital records.
findings.figures: 11 months, 8 months, 8 months overdue respectively; original targets June/October 2025; reset to September/December 2026
findings.quote: Concerns regarding the dependence on manual oversight, limited automation and lack of centralised digital monitoring will be addressed as part of the extensive operational improvements work currently being developed.

findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s174281/APPENDIX 1 - Red Risk Internal Audit Recommendations Update 2026-27 Q1.pdf
findings.headline: Business continuity exercise for cyber-attack not yet conducted; originally due September 2022.
findings.detail: 44 months overdue. Recommendation from June 2022 to repeat a cyber-attack BC exercise to test whether council's overall BC response capabilities have improved is not yet implemented. Exercise now planned for Q2 2026-27, reset to December 2026 with post-exercise review by March 2027. SME input from Internal Audit's co-sourced supplier being engaged.
findings.matters: No recent evidence of council's ability to maintain critical services during cyber incident. Lenders need confidence in operational resilience.
findings.figures: 44 months overdue; original target 30 September 2022; reset to 31 December 2026
findings.quote: There remains a lack of assurance the organisation's key risk management processes would be adequate and effective if / when needed.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 1 - Red Risk Internal Audit Recommendations Update 2026-27 Q1 , item 12.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s174281/APPENDIX 1 - Red Risk Internal Audit Recommendations Update 2026-27 Q1.pdf
findings.headline: Risk management system does not link risks to council corporate or service objectives; no Cabinet reporting on strategic risk.
findings.detail: Two related recommendations from June 2025 remain unimplemented. JCAD risk system does not link risks to objectives. No decision yet on Cabinet-level reporting on strategic risk. Risk reporting to Governance & Assurance Committee not yet reformed to include assurance-focused metrics (number of risks above tolerance, effectiveness of mitigations). All three recommendations reset to late 2026.
findings.matters: Without objectives-aligned risk reporting, Cabinet and lenders cannot assess how well the council understands and is managing its material risks.
findings.figures: 2 months overdue (as of June); three recommendations all reset to October/December 2026
findings.quote: The risk management system JCAD does not link the current risks to the (service or corporate) objectives to which they relate. Risk reporting seen at both strategic and operational levels remains framed around description of risks as written and not how they relate to established objectives.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX 1 - Red Risk Internal Audit Recommendations Update 2026-27 Q1 , item 12.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s174281/APPENDIX 1 - Red Risk Internal Audit Recommendations Update 2026-27 Q1.pdf
findings.headline: Budget overspends lack consistent, documented recovery action across the organisation.
findings.detail: A February 2026 recommendation to establish clear directive on forecast overspend mitigation remains partially implemented. Budget Playbook issued requiring Executive Directors to own and sign off mitigation plans, but M2 reporting shows further work needed. Follow-up not yet due; confidence flagged as Amber due to inherent difficulty in consistent implementation across directorates.
findings.matters: Forecast outturn risk material; absence of systematic mitigation planning means overspends can escalate without escalation or remedy.
findings.figures: 2 months overdue; original target 1 April 2026; reset to 31 July 2026
findings.quote: Clearer recovery action being taken but further work needed to ensure all forecast overspends have suitable recovery plans.

findings.headline: CIPFA Finance and Resilience Review identified 20 recommended actions on financial sustainability and governance; council is in multi-year EFS period.
findings.detail: CIPFA conducted a Finance and Resilience Review (2025/26) to evaluate the Council's financial sustainability, governance practices, and operational resilience. The review identified strengths, vulnerabilities, and significant challenges. CIPFA made 20 recommended actions for improvement. The Redbridge Recovery Board and Financial Strategy Board are monitoring these.
findings.matters: A CIPFA review with 20 recommendations on financial resilience signals deep concern about the council's sustainability. The sheer volume indicates structural, not cyclical, problems.
findings.figures: 20 recommended actions from CIPFA
findings.quote: A Finance and Resilience Review by CIPFA to evaluate the Council's financial sustainability, governance practices, and operational resilience. It provided insights into the Council's capacity to manage current financial pressures, meet statutory obligations, and support its strategic priorities amid ongoing economic and social challenges. The review identified strengths, potential vulnerabilities, and significant challenges to the Council's financial resilience. The review made 20 recommended actions where CIPFA deemed the Council should take the opportunity to improve.

findings.headline: Governance framework acknowledged as insufficient: 'some aspects of the Council's governance were found to be not sufficiently robustly designed or operating effectively in practice'.
findings.detail: The AGS states explicitly that during 2025/26 some aspects of governance were found not to be robustly designed or operating effectively, particularly in areas where external inspections found significant issues. The council has responded with enhancement actions but acknowledges gaps remain.
findings.matters: An admission that governance was not sufficiently robust is a material weakness. It suggests prior control failures and uncertainty about whether remediation is durable.
findings.figures: Areas identified: governance, audit, social care, SEND, housing
findings.quote: It is clear that during 2025/25 some aspects of the Council's governance were found to be not sufficiently robustly designed or operating effectively in practice. This was particularly the cases in those areas where external inspections found significant issues, risks, or weaknesses. The Council has responded strongly to these findings and is committed to ensuring the required improvements are made to service operation and the overall governance arrangements.

findings.headline: 231 Ombudsman complaints received in 2025/26, with 45 upheld and 44 referred back to council for local resolution.
findings.detail: The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman received 231 complaints and enquiries and issued 190 decisions. Of these, 45 complaints were upheld (representing service failure) and 44 cases were referred back to the council for local resolution. Housing, Education/Children's Services, and Adult Care accounted for the majority of findings against the council.
findings.matters: High upheld complaint and referral rates indicate service failures and poor first-resolution. This creates remediation costs, reputational risk, and suggests governance failures in service oversight.
findings.figures: 231 complaints, 190 decisions, 45 upheld, 44 referred back
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman received 231 complaints and enquiries relating to the Council and issued 190 decisions. Of these, 45 complaints were upheld and 44 cases were referred back to the Council for local resolution. Housing, Education and Children's Services and Adult Care Services accounted for the majority of findings against the Council.

findings.headline: External Auditor identified governance weakness in financial reporting and issued statutory recommendations to Full Council.
findings.detail: The External Auditor's Audit Report (26 February 2026) noted an 'Other Matter' regarding Governance, specifically financial reporting. On 9 March 2026, the auditor issued further recommendations designated as statutory and requiring reporting to Full Council. Details of specific issues are not provided in the AGS.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations on financial reporting governance suggest material weaknesses in financial control or disclosure. This directly undermines confidence in the integrity of the council's financial statements.
findings.figures: Recommendations issued 26 February 2026 and 9 March 2026
findings.quote: The External Auditor's Audit Report, dated 26 February 2026, set out an 'Other Matter' in relation to Governance, specifically in relation to financial reporting together with 'the action the Council must take to address the weakness'. Further to the Audit Report, the external auditor issued its Auditor's Annual Report on the 9 March 2026 making a further recommendation, in relation to Financial Reporting. The recommendations were designated as statutory recommendations which need to be reported to Full Council.

findings.headline: Very old audit recommendations remain overdue by 3–4.5 years, and implementation delays average 12 months past target.
findings.detail: The paper reports that recommendations are implemented on average 12 months after their original target date. A residual number of very old recommendations are aged 3–4.5 years past their target date. Whilst numbers over 7 and 12 months overdue decreased by year-end, the persistence of ancient overdue items signals slow remediation.
findings.matters: Audit recommendations that remain unaddressed for years indicate either weak oversight or resistance to change. This pattern suggests governance improvements may not stick, which affects confidence in any turnaround plan.
findings.figures: 3–4.5 years overdue for oldest recommendations; average 12 months delay
findings.quote: The timeliness of implementing recommendations remained broadly stable over the year, with recommendations being implemented on average 12 months after the original target date. There remains a residual number of very old recommendations being aged between three and four and a half years past target date.

findings.headline: OFSTED SEND inspection found 'widespread and/or systemic failings' requiring urgent action.
findings.detail: Although the Council maintained an outstanding rating for Children's Services in June 2024, a special inspection of the SEND local area partnership found widespread and systemic failings leading to significant concerns about outcomes for children and young people. A priority action plan was developed to address identified weaknesses.
findings.matters: SEND failures affect vulnerable children and expose the council to safeguarding liability, costly remediation, and reputational damage. The gap between the overall 'outstanding' rating and specific systemic failures in SEND highlights governance and oversight weaknesses.
findings.figures: Systemic failings identified; action plan in place
findings.quote: Although the Council maintained its outstanding rating from its Children's Services in June 2024, an inspection of the special educational needs and / or disabilities (SEND) Redbridge Local Area Partnership found that there were widespread and/or systemic failings leading to significant concerns about the experiences and outcomes of children and young people, which the local area partnership must address urgently.

findings.headline: CQC rated adult social care as 'requires improvement' with safeguarding and governance rated 'inadequate'.
findings.detail: In December 2025, the Care Quality Commission (CQC) conducted an inspection and rated the Council as requiring improvement in all nine areas assessed. Two areas — safeguarding and governance/management/sustainability — were rated 'inadequate', the lowest rating. CQC has notified the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care of the gaps requiring significant strengthening.
findings.matters: Inadequate governance and safeguarding ratings in a major spend area (social care) expose the council to legal, financial, and reputational risk. CQC notification to the Secretary of State escalates this beyond routine compliance.
findings.figures: Rating of 1 in some areas; inadequate in 2 of 9 areas assessed
findings.quote: In December 2025, the Care Quality Commission (CQC) rated the Council as requires improvement, in how well it is meeting its responsibilities to ensure people have access to adult social care and support under the Care Act (2014). CQC's assessment gave the quality Council services a rating of one in some areas. As a result of this, under Section 50(2) of the Health and Social Care Act 2008, CQC has sent a notification letter to the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care outlining the areas where improvements are needed.

findings.headline: Pattern of annual budget overspends in previous years shows the Council has been unable to manage financial challenges.
findings.detail: The effectiveness review explicitly notes that 'Overspends of annual budgets in previous years demonstrate that the Council has been unable to manage the many associated financial challenges it has faced and continues to face.' This pattern preceded the approval for EFS and signals underlying cost management problems.
findings.matters: A track record of overspends indicates structural budget management failure, not one-off pressures. This is directly relevant to a lender assessing whether the council can control expenditure and meet repayment obligations.
findings.figures: Not specified; described as 'previous years'
findings.quote: Overspends of annual budgets in previous years demonstrate that the Council has been unable to manage the many associated financial challenges it has faced and continues to face.

findings.headline: Council approved for multi-year Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) 2026/27–2029/30 due to unmanageable financial pressures.
findings.detail: The Council applied for and received government Exceptional Financial Support covering four years. The paper explicitly states the approval was for 'additional funding to manage pressures which have proved unmanageable' and enabled the Council to set a balanced budget for 2026/27. A Redbridge Recovery Board has been established with independent members and LGA representation to oversee the recovery plan.
findings.matters: EFS is a significant intervention signal; it indicates the council was unable to balance budgets through normal management and required government-backed support. This affects borrowing capacity and repayment credibility.
findings.figures: 2026/27–2029/30 (four-year settlement)
findings.quote: The Council's request for Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 – 2029/30 was approved by the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government in 2025/26. The Council can access additional funding to manage pressures which have proved unmanageable and this has enabled the Council to set a balanced budget for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Six interim or critical friend reviews undertaken in areas where management acknowledged limited assurance
findings.detail: In addition to formal audit opinions, the internal audit team completed six interim or critical friend reviews in areas where management acknowledged that the current internal control environment provided limited assurance. These covered waste disposal contracts, recruitment, temporary accommodation, service planning, adult social care quality assurance, and leisure contract management. This suggests councils are identifying control gaps before formal audit, but the gaps remain.
findings.matters: When management proactively acknowledges that control environments provide limited assurance and brings in auditors to help 'design in' controls, it signals that governance arrangements are immature or under strain. This affects financial control and service delivery risk across multiple areas.
findings.figures: Six interim critical friend reviews completed where management acknowledged limited assurance in: Waste disposal, Recruitment, TA, Leisure contract, Service planning, ASC QA
findings.quote: These were undertaken where the service's arrangements were developing and / or it was acknowledged by management the current internal control environment provided limited assurance. Therefore, the Internal Audit work conducted was to assist management with proactive forward-looking recommendations.

findings.headline: Cyber security controls rely on undocumented practices and individual judgment rather than formal requirements
findings.detail: The internal audit gave limited assurance on cyber security monitoring, detection and blocking. The assessment notes that cyber security tools and operational practices are in place but assurance is limited because there is current reliance on operational practices, technical configurations, and individual judgement rather than clearly documented organisational requirements, ownership, validation, and performance monitoring. A previous red-rated recommendation on business continuity exercising for cyber response has still not been implemented.
findings.matters: Undocumented security practices dependent on individual knowledge create operational risk and leave the council exposed if key personnel change. With cyber-attack risk rated red (15 vs target 10), this control weakness matters significantly.
findings.figures: CORP0011 (cyber-attack risk) red 15 vs target 10; cyber security recommended action not yet implemented
findings.quote: Assurance is limited as there is current reliance on operational practices, technical configurations, and individual judgement rather than clearly documented organisational requirements, ownership, validation, and performance monitoring. This recommended action is not yet implemented.

findings.headline: Multiple housing-related services showing limited assurance during period of high demand pressure
findings.detail: Internal audit gave limited assurance on housing allocations, housing supply new-build programme, and regeneration strategy. The strategic risk for reduction of affordable housing is rated red 16 (vs target 12) because demand for social housing in the borough remains high. Despite new director-level management and ongoing housing improvement programmes, the assurance levels remain limited.
findings.matters: High housing demand and limited assurance over delivery of new supply and allocations creates pressure on the council's temporary accommodation budgets and threatens its ability to prevent homelessness. These are both statutory duties and material budget risks.
findings.figures: Housing Allocations: Limited assurance; Housing Supply new-build: Limited assurance; CORP0014 (housing provision) red 16 vs target 12
findings.quote: The governance arrangements to be assured of the delivery of new build projects and the overall programme to time, budget, and targeted outcomes provided limited assurance. Despite exhaustive controls to manage the impact of this risk on the Council's finances, it remains red rated as demand for social housing in the Borough is high.

findings.headline: Transformation programme added to risk register Q4 2025/26 with rating 15 due to material risk of not delivering MTFS savings
findings.detail: The council's flagship modernisation programme was added to the strategic risk register in Q4 2025/26 specifically because there is a high-likelihood risk that it will not deliver the savings expected in the Medium Term Financial Strategy. Although the council is investing significant resources in operationalising the programme and has applied for exceptional financial support (now granted), the transformation programme failure risk is rated red 15 with likelihood 5 (certain) and impact 3 (significant).
findings.matters: If the transformation programme—which the council is relying on for efficiency savings to address financial pressures—fails to deliver, the council will have no secondary mitigation for its financial resilience challenges and may face a deepening deficit.
findings.figures: CORP0038 residual rating 15 (likelihood 5 certain, impact 3 significant); added to risk register Q4 2025/26
findings.quote: This risk was added to the risk register Q4 2025/26 to highlight the strategic importance of the modernisation programme to the Council's medium and long term sustainability. Whilst the flagship programme is an opportunity to digitise and streamline Council services to achieve efficiency savings, this opportunity also carries risk as expressed by the risk cause.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand outstripping budget despite multiple controls in place
findings.detail: The council's highest-rated red strategic risk is demand for Adult Social Care outstripping available budgets (rating 25 vs target 16). Despite pay control panels scrutinising staffing expenditure and savings targets being in place, the high demand for the council's social care services continues and the residual rating remains unchanged. Internal audit identified reasonable progress on forecasting improvements but notes that some variables driving complexity, length and cost of care could be expanded.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically the largest budget item for local authorities and uncontrolled demand growth directly threatens financial sustainability. The council's inability to bring this risk within tolerance despite a year of mitigation efforts suggests the problem is structural.
findings.figures: CORP0032 residual rating 25 (likelihood 5 almost certain, impact 5 severe), target 16
findings.quote: The high demand for the Council's social care services is ongoing and consequently the red residual rating of this risk is unchanged this quarter. The residual rating is 25 (red), with a likelihood 5 (almost certain) and an impact of 5 (severe)

findings.headline: Limited assurance over financial management controls for expenditure and income
findings.detail: The internal audit gave limited assurance on financial management arrangements for controlling expenditure and for managing income, specifically flagging that housing rent management information and reporting functionality in Civica limits assurance. The audit notes that corporate internal control arrangements do not consistently ensure service area budget holders identify robust, deliverable mitigating actions for forecast overspends.
findings.matters: Limited assurance over expenditure controls and income management directly undermines the council's ability to respond to budget pressures and to track whether services are staying within budget. This is critical given the council's reported financial resilience challenges.
findings.figures: Financial management – controlling expenditure: Limited assurance; Financial management – managing income (Housing Rents): Limited assurance
findings.quote: The corporate internal control and governance arrangements that were in place during the fieldwork period in 2025/26 Q1/Q2 to respond to forecast overspends does not consistently provide assurance that service area budget holders promptly identify robust, deliverable mitigating actions capable of minimising or eliminating forecast overspends.

findings.headline: Red-rated audit recommendations delayed years past target date, some by 17 months or more
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2026, 12 red-rated recommendations remain past their original target implementation date. The report shows recommendations from Q3 (reported January 2026) were implemented 16 months after target, Q1 (July 2025) were 17 months late, and one cyber security recommendation is 3.5 years past agreed target. This means identified control weaknesses remain unaddressed for extended periods.
findings.matters: Delayed implementation of red-rated recommendations means the council is tolerating identified control weaknesses—particularly financial controls and business continuity—for longer than management acknowledged as acceptable, increasing the risk of loss or failure.
findings.figures: 12 red-rated recommendations past target as at 31 March 2026; Q3 recommendations implemented 16 months late; Q1 recommendations 17 months late; one cyber recommendation 3.5 years past target
findings.quote: Red risk recommendations brought forward 1 April 2025: 18; new red risk recommendations made during 2025/26: +23; red risk recommendations past original target date 31 March 2026: 12. Time past original target date of current outstanding recommendations (12) = 3 at >12 months past target

findings.headline: Six strategic risks rated red, with four above the council's tolerable risk level
findings.detail: The council has identified six strategic risks with high residual risk ratings. Four of these are above the council's target tolerance level, including Adult Social Care demand outstripping budgets (rating 25 vs target 16), cyber-attack risk (rating 15 vs target 10), and the transformation programme failing to deliver MTFS savings (rating 15 vs target 6). The audit report notes that further strengthening of mitigations is needed to bring these within tolerance.
findings.matters: Red-rated strategic risks above tolerance indicate the council is exposed to significant impacts that it may not be able to manage effectively. This directly affects financial sustainability and the council's ability to meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: CORP0032 (ASC): 25 vs target 16; CORP0011 (Cyber): 15 vs target 10; CORP0038 (Transformation): 15 vs target 6; CORP0014 (Housing): 16 vs target 12
findings.quote: The Council also recognises that it is several strategic risks with a high residual risk level above its targeted, tolerable level, indicating that further strengthening of the mitigations are needed.

findings.detail: EY flagged that in-year whistleblowing is not being dealt with in an appropriate manner by management. This is listed among significant value for money risks in the audit.
findings.matters: Suggests governance and internal control weaknesses; may indicate management is not responding appropriately to staff concerns or misconduct reports
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: In year Whistleblowing not being dealt with in an appropriate manner b y Management.

findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s174282/Annual Audit Results Report Action Plan Update - Report.pdf
findings.headline: Staff turnover exposed fragility in accounting practices, working shortcuts and outdated financial systems
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that turnover of finance staff has exposed inadequate and outdated accounting practices and working shortcuts. While the council states these issues do not affect key numbers in the accounts or reserve balances, the auditor escalated recommendations to statutory level, and the council is undertaking a longer-term improvement plan and financial system upgrade.
findings.matters: Shows control weaknesses in financial reporting and suggests the council's finance function was fragile; raises questions about data reliability even if key numbers are unaffected
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The turnover of staff has exposed the fragility of working practices and use of shortcuts and workarounds. It has also exposed inadequate and out of date accounting practices and systems.

findings.paper_title: Annual Audit Results Report 2024/25 - Action Plan Update
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s174282/Annual Audit Results Report Action Plan Update - Report.pdf
findings.headline: Council overspent in 2024/25 and is forecasting significant overspends for 2025/26, with increasing budget gaps for 2026/27 and beyond
findings.detail: The external auditor (EY) identified this as a significant value for money risk. The council is not only in deficit this year but expects the position to worsen, with identified gaps in future years. The document provides no detail on the size of the overspend or gaps.
findings.matters: Shows the council is spending beyond its means and the problem is deteriorating; critical for lenders assessing the council's financial trajectory and sustainability
findings.figures: Council overspent in 2024/25; significant overspends forecasted 2025/26; increasing budget gaps identified 2026/27 onwards (no amounts stated)
findings.quote: The Council overspent in 2024/25, is forecasting significant overspends for 2025/26 and has identified increasing budget gaps for 2026/27 and beyond.

findings.headline: SEND inspection triggered unbudgeted urgent improvements creating additional education pressures
findings.detail: The Education and Inclusion overspend of £2.147m includes unbudgeted costs for urgent SEND improvements following a recent inspection. Inspection recommendations are mandatory and will create ongoing budget pressure.
findings.matters: Inspection-driven improvements are non-discretionary and cannot be avoided or deferred. Combined with existing staffing and demand pressures, this indicates the council's education service is under sustained stress.
findings.figures: £2.147m overspend in Education and Inclusion (on £16.329m outturn); part of broader £67.797m Children and Education directorate overspend
findings.quote: Reasons for the overspend include unbudgeted urgent improvements needed in SEND following the recent inspection

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £9.134m; swing from £5.490m surplus to deficit in one year
findings.detail: The DSG, which is ring-fenced but must eventually be recovered from the General Fund, moved from a brought-forward surplus of £5.490m to an accumulated deficit of £9.134m due to £14.624m overspend. This represents a swing of £14.624m in a single year and creates a future liability.
findings.matters: DSG deficits cannot be carried indefinitely and will force either service cuts or General Fund support to clear. The scale and speed of deterioration suggests structural problems in schools funding or SEND costs.
findings.figures: £14.624m DSG overspend on £333.243m budget; deficit swing from +£5.490m to -£9.134m
findings.quote: The DSG reserve brought forward on 1st April 2025 was a surplus of £5.490m. An in-year deficit of £14.624m resulted in a reserve deficit of £9.134m at the end of FY 25/26.

findings.headline: Savings programme delivers only 67%; £6.295m of undelivered savings simply reversed rather than replaced
findings.detail: The council planned £21.815m of savings but only delivered £14.448m (67%). The remaining £7.367m was not delivered, and crucially, £6.295m of this was reversed rather than replaced with alternative savings. This shows the council cannot manage its expenditure or find offsetting savings.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver or replace savings demonstrates loss of expenditure control and suggests future budget positions will deteriorate as planned efficiencies fail to materialise.
findings.figures: £21.815m savings target; £14.448m delivered (67% rate); £6.295m reversed for 2026/27 without replacement
findings.quote: Total savings to be delivered in 2025/26 were £21.815m, at outturn £14.448m of these savings were delivered. Of the remaining £7.367m undelivered savings...the remaining £6.295m were reversed as part of the budget setting for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £23.283m with unattainable income targets and rising care costs
findings.detail: The Adults directorate overspend of £23.283m reflects sustained cost pressures in care purchasing, staffing costs, and income that the council cannot collect as forecast. This is the second-largest service pressure and indicates ongoing demand-led growth in a statutory service.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a mandatory service with demographic growth driving costs. Unattainable income targets suggest budget planning assumptions are unrealistic and will not be corrected.
findings.figures: £23.283m overspend on £88.175m budget (26% overspend); second largest directorate pressure
findings.quote: predominately due to rising costs within care purchasing, staffing cost pressures, unattainable income and backdated uplifts within Adults Social Care.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs of £21.443m driven by uncontrolled demand and housing shortage
findings.detail: The Place directorate's £21.443m overspend is the single largest pressure, described as predominantly driven by temporary accommodation demand coupled with escalating housing costs from supply shortage. This is a structural, demand-led pressure that the council cannot control or contain.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory obligation that grows with homelessness and cannot be cut. The housing shortage driving costs is unlikely to resolve quickly, meaning this pressure will persist.
findings.figures: £21.443m overspend (65% of £32.740m budget); Place directorate accounts for 80% of total General Fund overspend
findings.quote: predominately due to the increasing demand for temporary accommodation (TA), coupled with escalating housing costs (driven by a shortage in supply), which has led to a continued increase in overall cost.

findings.paper_title: To receive and consider a report from officers entitled "Review of the Housing Revenue Account Finances and HRA Budget 2026/27 to 2030/31"
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s173074/Housing Revenue Account Finances and Rent Setting - Report.pdf
findings.headline: Government rent convergence policy resumes from 2027/28, constraining rent-setting discretion to £1-£2 per week increments
findings.detail: From 2027/28, rent convergence will resume at £1/week, rising to £2/week from 2028/29. This caps the council's ability to increase rents above these convergence increments regardless of inflation or cost growth.
findings.matters: Rent convergence policy creates a structural revenue gap if inflation exceeds the £1-£2/week increments, with no mitigation path identified in the paper.
findings.figures: Convergence increments: £1/week (2027/28), £2/week (2028/29 onwards)
findings.quote: It was confirmed on 28 January 2026 that convergence will resume from 2027/28 initially at the rate of £1 per week, rising to £2 per week from 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: To receive and consider a report from officers entitled "Review of the Housing Revenue Account Finances and HRA Budget 2026/27 to 2030/31"
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s173074/Housing Revenue Account Finances and Rent Setting - Report.pdf
findings.headline: HRA must borrow an additional £101.228m over 2026/27 to 2030/31 to fund the capital programme
findings.detail: The paper states the HRA will need to borrow £101.228m between 2026/27 and 2030/31 to fund capital investment, in addition to existing 2012 self-financing debt. While the 30-year business plan projects sustainability, this represents material new debt servicing obligations.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the HRA's revenue base and reserves can sustain higher debt levels if interest rates rise above the assumed 4.24% for 2026/27.
findings.figures: £101.228m additional borrowing required; interest costs at 4.24% (2026/27), declining to 3.89% (2030/31+)
findings.quote: To fund the capital programme over the next 5 years it will be necessary for the HRA to borrow an additional £101.228m between 2026/27 and 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: To receive and consider a report from officers entitled "Revenue and Capital Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and MTFS 2026/27- 2030/31"
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.redbridge.gov.uk/documents/s173077/Revenue Capital Budget and Council Tax 26 -27 and MTFS 26-27 and 30-31 - Report.pdf
findings.headline: Reserves depleted annually with multi-year recovery plan not yet fully funded or secured
findings.detail: The S151 Officer notes 'considerable utilisation of reserves forecast in 2025/26' and states 'more difficult decisions are likely to need to be made in the coming years to balance the annual out-turn of the General Fund without the use of reserves'. Neither the General Fund Balance nor Business Risk Reserve is forecast to be at target level for 2026/27, requiring 'a number of years to replenish'. This creates ongoing structural deficit.
findings.matters: Using reserves every year masks structural imbalance. If reserves are not replenished while being depleted, the council is living beyond its means and moving toward insolvency.

news_drafts.headline: Redbridge still relies on exceptional financial support, aiming to end that need beyond 2028/29
news_drafts.lead:
Redbridge Council says it is still reliant on exceptional financial support (EFS), government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, while it rebuilds its financial resilience. Its Cabinet papers for 12 November say the council aims to reduce that reliance over the next three years, so that it has no need for support beyond 2028/29.

The quarter 2 budget control report for 2026/27 says the council's modernisation programme is funded by EFS borrowing. Modernisation spend is forecast at £4.310m for 2026/27. The report describes the council as "still reliant on EFS whilst it rebuilds its financial resilience".

The council's mid-year treasury management report says its 2026/27 borrowing requirement includes borrowing for EFS, alongside borrowing for capital spending. It says additional external borrowing will be needed for both, "as well as to fund borrowing for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)". EFS borrowing must comply with the terms of the applicable capitalisation direction, the government permission to treat day-to-day spending as if it were capital spending so it can be paid for by borrowing or asset sales. The treasury paper gives no amount for EFS borrowing.

news_drafts.headline: Redbridge treasury review says borrowing will be needed for exceptional financial support, with no amount given
news_drafts.lead:
Redbridge's mid-year treasury management review, before the Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 9 November 2026, says the council will need to borrow to fund exceptional financial support (EFS). EFS is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The paper states no amount for this borrowing.

Paragraph 6.11 says borrowing will be needed "as well as to fund borrowing for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)". It describes this as in addition to borrowing for maturing debt and for the capital programme.

Paragraph 21.2 says any borrowing related to EFS must comply with the terms of the applicable capitalisation direction, which is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so that borrowing can pay for it. It must also meet capital finance requirements and the rules on minimum revenue provision, the amount a council must set aside from each year's budget to pay off past borrowing.

news_drafts.headline: Redbridge's net borrowing rose £119.487m to £447.371m, 36% increase; PWLB borrowing to end 2027 onwards with no further planned access
news_drafts.lead: Redbridge council's net borrowing increased by £119.487m to £447.371m in the year to March 2026, a 36 per cent rise driven partly by higher interest rates on new loans. The council took £85m of new Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) borrowing—the government's lending arm for councils—at an average cost of 2.89 per cent for general services, but will take only £25m more PWLB funding in 2026/27 before ending access entirely. The council's papers show no further PWLB borrowing is planned from 2027 onwards, signalling either that its government lending capacity is exhausted or a deliberate shift to market financing. To manage the debt without borrowing more externally, the council deployed £94.934m of its own cash reserves as a substitute for loans, reducing investment balances from £143.8m to £116.8m. The average cost of borrowing rose to 3.53 per cent from 3.43 per cent.
